content.comment_body: Hello! I have an old [article_no] that seems to have a similar issue—losing date and time after a power failure. How have others resolved this?
Did you only read the original post, or also the replies from other users? The answers have already been provided.

Hi, I did read all the posts. The thread started back in 2013, so maybe back then it was easier to buy a memory or battery card. Nowadays, it's more difficult to find one. Is this issue common or normal for [version_no]? Do these devices typically lose or damage the RTC buffer after a power failure?

Yes. How long the clock is buffered during power loss depends on the specific series. Is your question about the product in general or about a specific [version_no]? If so, please specify which one you want information about—whether [article_no], [article_no], or [article_no].

I am using a [version_no] Series. The weekly timer's help section says this series can retain RTC for 80 hours, and that duration is affected by ambient temperature. My question is whether it is normal for the buffer to fail.
What exactly do you mean by 'is it normal for the buffer to fail'?
After several years of use, both the original poster and I have devices that no longer retain RTC during power outages. Is it common, after years of usage, for the buffer to eventually fail?
I can't say whether this is normal, as I'm not sure. In your situation, I would recommend creating a support request.

If the device loses date and time even after a short power outage, it may be defective. This is not standard behavior. For instance, my [version_no] (without battery module) still keeps correct date and time even after a weekend without power.

Hello, All versions of the [product_name] RTC are powered by a super-capacitor, which takes a long time to fully charge. I recommend keeping the device powered for at least 24 hours before testing again. I've never heard of a super-capacitor losing capacity entirely. I have a [version_no] that has been used for around 20 years, only occasionally switched off, and the date/time has always remained valid. The typical power outage it handles is very brief, usually less than an hour. Hope this information helps.

I agree that a minimum of 24 hours of power is needed to charge the super-capacitor if it is fully drained. My [product_name] is typically powered all week except weekends. In my experience, if it's switched off after 8 hours of charging, the date and time are still correct the following day. So sometimes a shorter power period works too, but expect less buffer time. If your device loses its date and time, you can also update it from your PC using [product_name] software.

analysis.insight_summary: Forum users are concerned with [product_name] ([version_no]) losing date and time after power interruptions. These discussions raise questions about whether it is normal for the RTC backup to degrade after years of operation, given that documentation states the RTC should retain time up to 80 hours. Some comments clarify that such loss of time is not typical, and one user notes the RTC uses a super-capacitor which may need a long charging period to work properly.
analysis.user_expectations: Users expect the [product_name] ([version_no]) to maintain accurate date and time through power outages for the stated 80-hour duration, even after several years in use.
